hypotheses.title: Missing deadline enforcement allows stale swap execution
hypotheses.description: The router passes `deadline: block.timestamp` to the Slipstream SwapRouter's `exactInput`, which means the deadline is always satisfied at the moment of execution. There is no user-supplied deadline parameter, so a transaction that sits in the mempool (or is executed by a malicious validator/MEV bot) can be included at any future time with the same `minTrustOut` value, exposing the user to price movement between signing and inclusion.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User submits `swapAndBridgeWithETH` with a `minTrustOut` computed at current prices. 2) A searcher/validator holds the tx and waits for TRUST price to drop (or WETH to rise). 3) Tx is included later; the swap still executes because `deadline == block.timestamp` is trivially satisfied. 4) User receives fewer TRUST than intended (bounded only by `minTrustOut`, which the user may have set loosely).
hypotheses.impact: Users can be sandwiched / executed at stale prices, receiving less TRUST than expected; loss of value on every swap.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an explicit `deadline` parameter to both swap functions and pass it through to `exactInput` instead of `block.timestamp`.

hypotheses.title: TrustSwapAndBridgeRouter uses block.timestamp as swap deadline
hypotheses.description: Both swap functions pass `deadline: block.timestamp` to the Slipstream router. This provides no meaningful deadline protection: the transaction is always valid at the moment it executes, so a validator/MEV searcher can hold the transaction and include it at any future block where the swap is still profitable to them, extracting value from the user via sandwiching or delayed execution. The user's only protection is `minTrustOut`, but the deadline parameter is effectively a no-op.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User submits swapAndBridgeWithETH with a reasonable minTrustOut. 2) A searcher observes the pending tx, holds it, and manipulates the pool price (or waits for adverse price movement) so the swap executes at a worse rate that still satisfies minTrustOut but extracts value. 3) Because deadline == block.timestamp at inclusion, the tx never reverts for staleness.
hypotheses.impact: Users suffer worse execution than intended; MEV extraction; loss of funds relative to fair execution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Accept a user-supplied `deadline` parameter and pass it through to the Slipstream router.

hypotheses.title: Utilization rollover lets users double-count deposits across epochs
hypotheses.description: `_rollover` copies the previous epoch's `totalUtilization` and `personalUtilization` into the current epoch whenever the current epoch's value is still zero. Because `_addUtilization`/`_removeUtilization` call `_rollover` before mutating, a user who was active in epoch N-1 but inactive in epoch N will have their old utilization silently re-credited to epoch N on their first action. The same applies system-wide: the first depositor of a new epoch re-seeds `totalUtilization[currentEpoch]` from the prior epoch, so the "delta" used by TrustBonding's utilization ratio is inflated.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits a large amount in epoch N-1, creating a large `personalUtilization[N-1]` and `totalUtilization[N-1]`. 2) Attacker does nothing for the rest of epoch N-1 and into epoch N. 3) In epoch N, attacker performs a tiny deposit (or redeem) — `_rollover` copies the old utilization into epoch N. 4) TrustBonding's `_getPersonalUtilizationRatio` computes `userUtilizationAfter - userUtilizationBefore` using the rolled-over value, which is now large relative to the target, yielding 100% ratio and full rewards. 5) Attacker claims rewards for epoch N-1 (and subsequent epochs) at maximum ratio despite not having deposited in those epochs.
hypotheses.impact: Rewards are distributed to users who did not actually contribute utilization in the epoch, diluting honest participants and potentially draining the emissions pool faster than intended. System utilization ratio is also inflated, causing over-emission.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not roll over utilization into a new epoch; instead, treat a user's utilization in an epoch as zero unless they explicitly acted in that epoch, and compute deltas against the actual prior-epoch value without copying.

hypotheses.title: TrustBonding claimRewards double-counts personal utilization target
hypotheses.description: `_getPersonalUtilizationRatio` uses `userClaimedRewardsForEpoch[account][epoch-1]` as the "target utilization" for the current epoch. But `claimRewards` writes `userClaimedRewardsForEpoch[msg.sender][prevEpoch] = userRewards` (the already-utilization-scaled amount), not the raw eligible rewards. This means the target is the discounted amount, so a user who claimed a discounted reward last epoch has a smaller target, making `userUtilizationDelta >= userUtilizationTarget` easier to satisfy and inflating the next epoch's ratio toward 100%. The accounting drifts from the intended "target = raw eligible rewards" semantics.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker locks TRUST and deposits into MultiVault to build utilization. 2) Claims rewards in epoch N, storing a discounted `userClaimedRewardsForEpoch[N]`. 3) In epoch N+1, `_getPersonalUtilizationRatio` compares delta against the discounted target, returning 100% more often than intended. 4) Attacker repeatedly claims at max ratio, extracting more emissions than their true utilization warrants.
hypotheses.impact: Over-distribution of TRUST emissions; protocol reward pool drained faster than intended; other users' pro-rata rewards diluted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Store the raw eligible rewards (pre-utilization) as the target, or compute the target from `_userEligibleRewardsForEpoch(account, epoch-1)` rather than the claimed amount.

hypotheses.title: TrustBonding rewards claimable window can be griefed via utilization manipulation
hypotheses.description: The personal utilization ratio for a user in epoch N is computed from `getUserUtilizationInEpoch(user, N-1)` and `getUserUtilizationInEpoch(user, N)`. `MultiVault.getUserUtilizationInEpoch` reverts with `MultiVault_EpochNotTracked` if the user has no tracked epoch history at or before the requested epoch. A user who has never interacted with MultiVault (or whose 3-slot history has rolled past the queried epoch) will cause `_getPersonalUtilizationRatio` to revert, blocking `claimRewards` entirely.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker locks TRUST in TrustBonding to accrue veTRUST rewards. 2) Attacker never calls MultiVault deposit/redeem, so `userEpochHistory[attacker]` stays empty. 3) When `claimRewards` is called for the previous epoch, `_getPersonalUtilizationRatio` calls `getUserUtilizationInEpoch(attacker, prevEpoch-1)` which reverts with `MultiVault_EpochNotTracked`. 4) Rewards are permanently unclaimable for that epoch.
hypotheses.impact: Users who bond TRUST but never interact with MultiVault cannot claim any rewards; their emissions are stuck in SatelliteEmissionsController and eventually reclaimed/bridged away, causing loss of earned rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `_getPersonalUtilizationRatio`, wrap the `getUserUtilizationInEpoch` calls in try/catch and default to `BASIS_POINTS_DIVISOR` (or the lower bound) when the epoch is not tracked, rather than reverting.

hypotheses.title: MultiVault approvals are not scoped to termId or curveId
hypotheses.description: `approve(sender, approvalType)` grants blanket deposit/redemption approval across all terms and curves. A user who approves a sender for a single deposit inadvertently authorizes that sender to deposit on their behalf into any term/curve, and to redeem any of their shares in any vault. There is no per-term or per-curve scoping, and no expiry. An approved sender can drain the receiver's shares across all vaults via `redeem`/`redeemBatch`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim calls `approve(attacker, ApprovalTypes.REDEMPTION)` intending to allow a single redemption. 2) Attacker calls `redeem(victim, anyTermId, anyCurveId, victimShares, 0)` for every vault the victim holds shares in. 3) Attacker receives all assets; victim loses all shares.
hypotheses.impact: Complete loss of the victim's vault shares and underlying assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Scope approvals to (termId, curveId) or add per-approval expiry and amount limits.

hypotheses.title: Unclaimed emissions can be withdrawn and bridged for the same epoch
hypotheses.description: Both `withdrawUnclaimedEmissions` and `bridgeUnclaimedEmissions` guard against re-use via `_reclaimedEmissions[epoch] > 0`, but they share the same mapping. The check is `> 0`, so if `getUnclaimedRewardsForEpoch(epoch)` returns a value that is later reduced (e.g., because a user claims rewards for that epoch after the admin withdrew), the mapping still holds the old amount and blocks further withdrawals — that part is fine. The real issue is the reverse: `getUnclaimedRewardsForEpoch` returns `epochRewards - totalClaimedRewardsForEpoch[epoch]`, and `totalClaimedRewardsForEpoch` is only incremented in `TrustBonding.claimRewards`. If the admin withdraws unclaimed emissions for epoch N, then a user claims for epoch N afterwards, the user's claim succeeds (TrustBonding has no knowledge of the withdrawal), so the same emissions are paid out twice: once to the admin's recipient and once to the user.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Epoch N ends with unclaimed rewards. 2) Admin (or OPERATOR) calls `withdrawUnclaimedEmissions(N, recipient)` — funds sent out, `_reclaimedEmissions[N]` set. 3) A user who was eligible for epoch N calls `TrustBonding.claimRewards` — `_hasClaimedRewardsForEpoch` is false, so the claim succeeds and `totalClaimedRewardsForEpoch[N]` is incremented. 4) The SatelliteEmissionsController pays the user from its balance, which was already reduced by the admin withdrawal. If balance is insufficient, the user's claim reverts (funds frozen); if balance is sufficient (from other epochs), the same epoch's emissions are paid twice.
hypotheses.impact: Double payment of emissions for the same epoch, draining the SatelliteEmissionsController balance and potentially making later legitimate claims revert (frozen funds).
hypotheses.recommendation: Have `withdrawUnclaimedEmissions`/`bridgeUnclaimedEmissions` mark the epoch as fully claimed in TrustBonding (e.g., set `totalClaimedRewardsForEpoch[epoch] = epochRewards`) so subsequent user claims for that epoch revert.

hypotheses.title: TrustBonding claimRewards reverts when user has no MultiVault history
hypotheses.description: `getUserCurrentClaimableRewards` calls `_getPersonalUtilizationRatio(account, prevEpoch)` which internally calls `IMultiVault.getUserUtilizationInEpoch`. For accounts with no MultiVault activity, this reverts with `MultiVault_EpochNotTracked`, making the view function unusable and any integrator relying on it (frontends, other contracts) fail.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any external caller invoking `getUserCurrentClaimableRewards` for a fresh veTRUST holder triggers a revert, breaking integrations and preventing users from discovering their claimable rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Broken view function; downstream integrations (UI, claim aggregators) fail; users cannot determine claimable amounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Same as above — handle the untracked-epoch case gracefully in `_getPersonalUtilizationRatio`.

hypotheses.title: MultiVault getUserUtilizationInEpoch returns wrong epoch's utilization
hypotheses.description: The function checks `if (_userEpochHistory[0] <= epoch)` and returns `personalUtilization[user][_userEpochHistory[0]]`. This is incorrect: if the user's most recent active epoch is less than or equal to the requested epoch, the function returns the utilization for the most recent active epoch, not for the requested epoch. For example, if the user was last active in epoch 5 and the caller requests epoch 10, the function returns the utilization for epoch 5, which is wrong. The correct behavior should be to return the utilization for the requested epoch if it exists, or the most recent epoch's utilization if the requested epoch is after the last active epoch (since utilization rolls forward). The current logic returns the wrong value whenever the requested epoch is greater than the user's last active epoch.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes that `getUserUtilizationInEpoch` returns stale utilization for epochs after their last activity. 2) TrustBonding uses this function to compute personal utilization ratios for reward calculations. 3) The attacker can manipulate their activity pattern to ensure the function returns a favorable (inflated) utilization for the epoch being evaluated, increasing their rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect utilization values lead to incorrect reward calculations in TrustBonding, potentially draining the emissions pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Return `personalUtilization[user][epoch]` when `epoch` is within the tracked history, and handle the rollover case explicitly.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.changeController has no access control
hypotheses.description: `changeController(address _newController)` only checks `msg.sender == controller` but `controller` is set to `_admin` in `__VotingEscrow_init`. However, the function is not gated by any role and the `controller` variable is a plain public state variable that can be set to any address. More critically, the function has no `onlyRole` modifier and the check `msg.sender == controller` is the only guard. Since `controller` is initialized to the admin address, this is effectively admin-only, but the function is a leftover Aragon compatibility stub that bypasses the AccessControl system entirely. If `controller` is ever set to a non-admin address (e.g., via this same function by the admin), that address gains unilateral control. The real issue is that this function exists outside the AccessControl framework and can be used to transfer control to an arbitrary address without emitting events or going through the role system.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Admin calls `changeController(attacker)` (or controller is set to a contract that can be manipulated). 2. Attacker now controls `controller`. 3. Attacker can call `changeController` again to maintain control. However, since only the admin can initially set controller, this requires admin action. The actual vulnerability is that `controller` is a separate trust path from `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` — if the admin role is revoked from an address but that address is still `controller`, it retains control over `changeController`.
hypotheses.impact: Bypass of the AccessControl role system; a stale controller address retains privileged access even after admin role revocation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove `changeController` or gate it with `onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE)` and sync it with the role system.

hypotheses.title: MultiVault _increaseProRataVaultsAssets loses dust to contract
hypotheses.description: `amountPerTerm = amount / 3` truncates, and the remainder (up to 2 wei per call) is never credited to any vault. The comment acknowledges this, but the dust accumulates in the MultiVault contract balance without being tracked in any vault's `totalAssets`. Over many triple creations/deposits, this creates a persistent mismatch between the contract's TRUST balance and the sum of vault `totalAssets`, which can be swept or mis-accounted.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker repeatedly triggers triple deposits/creations that invoke `_increaseProRataVaultsAssets` with amounts not divisible by 3. 2) Each call leaves 1-2 wei of untracked TRUST in the contract. 3) Over time the untracked balance grows; any future logic that assumes `balance == sum(totalAssets)` (e.g., migration, sweeps) is off.
hypotheses.impact: Small but permanent accounting drift between real holdings and vault totals; potential for future invariant violations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Distribute the remainder to one of the three vaults (e.g., subject) instead of discarding it.

hypotheses.title: quoteExactInput uses non-view quoter callable by anyone, no staleness check
hypotheses.description: `quoteExactInput` is declared non-view and calls the Slipstream Quoter, swallowing all reverts and returning 0. Off-chain integrators relying on this quote get no signal that the quote failed (0 is indistinguishable from a legitimate zero output), and there is no timestamp/block check to detect stale pool state. Because the function is non-view, it cannot be used safely in on-chain integrations that expect a view.
hypotheses.attackPath: An integrator calls `quoteExactInput` off-chain to size a swap; if the pool is paused, illiquid, or the quoter reverts, the function silently returns 0. The integrator then submits a swap with `minTrustOut = 0`, which the router accepts, and the swap executes at whatever price the pool offers.
hypotheses.impact: Silent zero quotes lead to swaps with no slippage protection; users can be drained by MEV/sandwich attacks.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make the function `view`, revert on quoter failure (or return a sentinel), and require callers to pass a nonzero `minTrustOut`.

hypotheses.title: TrustBonding utilization ratio uses uninitialized epoch data for first claims
hypotheses.description: For epochs 0 and 1 the function returns `BASIS_POINTS_DIVISOR` (100%) unconditionally, and for later epochs it reads `getUserUtilizationInEpoch(_account, _epoch - 1)` and `_epoch`. If a user has no tracked epoch history (e.g., they never interacted with MultiVault), `getUserUtilizationInEpoch` reverts with `MultiVault_EpochNotTracked`, causing `claimRewards` to revert for users who locked TRUST but never deposited into MultiVault. This is a griefing/DoS vector on reward claims.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user locks TRUST via `create_lock` but never calls MultiVault deposit/redeem. When they call `claimRewards`, `_getPersonalUtilizationRatio` calls `getUserUtilizationInEpoch` which reverts because `userEpochHistory` is empty, blocking the claim. An attacker cannot directly exploit this, but any user in this state is permanently unable to claim rewards until they interact with MultiVault.
hypotheses.impact: Users with locked TRUST but no MultiVault history cannot claim rewards; funds (rewards) effectively frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Handle the `MultiVault_EpochNotTracked` revert gracefully by treating missing history as zero utilization and returning the lower bound or 100%.

hypotheses.title: WrappedTrust.withdraw lacks reentrancy guard, allows uint underflow drain
hypotheses.description: `withdraw` performs the external `Address.sendValue` call to `msg.sender` and only decrements `balanceOf` afterward. Solidity 0.8.x does enforce underflow checks, so a naive reentrancy on the same withdraw would revert, but the interaction pattern still breaks the intended accounting: an attacker can reenter `withdraw` (or `transfer`/`transferFrom`) before the balance is reduced, observing the stale balance. Worse, reentering `deposit` mid-`withdraw` and re-borrowing control means the sendValue call happens before state mutation, an ordering violation the codebase otherwise guards against.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker contract calls `withdraw(x)`. 2) Inside `Address.sendValue`, the fallback of the attacker reenters `withdraw(x)` again before `balanceOf[msg.sender] -= amount` executes. 3) With Solidity 0.8 underflow, the second inner call succeeds only if balance is still `>= x`, so attacker drains in nested calls before the outer write lands; then outer write also executes, decrementing again, effectively double-spending the same balance if `sendValue` reverts partway. 4) Alternatively reenter `transfer` to send to a fresh address while original balance is intact.
hypotheses.impact: Double-spend / draining of WTRUST balances and irrecoverable ETH accounting errors; breaks totalSupply invariant vs ETH held.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply checks-effects-interactions: decrement `balanceOf[msg.sender]` before the `sendValue` call, and add a `nonReentrant` guard.

hypotheses.title: MultiVault redeem blocked when remaining shares fall below minShare
hypotheses.description: `_validateRedeem` reverts if `remainingShares < generalConfig.minShare`. Because `minShare` is minted to `BURN_ADDRESS` on vault creation, the burn address's shares are never redeemable. If a vault's total shares ever equal exactly `minShare` (e.g., all non-burn holders redeem), the last real holder cannot redeem their shares because doing so would leave `remainingShares < minShare`. Their funds are permanently stuck.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a vault with minimal deposit. 2) Other users deposit and later redeem, leaving only the attacker's shares plus the burn-address minShare. 3) Attacker attempts to redeem; `remainingShares = minShare - attackerShares < minShare` reverts. 4) Attacker's assets are locked in the vault forever.
hypotheses.impact: Last remaining shareholder cannot withdraw; assets permanently locked in the vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow redemption down to `minShare` (i.e., require `remainingShares >= minShare` only when the redeemer is not the last non-burn holder), or exclude burn-address shares from the check.

hypotheses.title: TrustSwapAndBridgeRouter path validation allows arbitrary intermediate tokens
hypotheses.description: `_validatePoolsExist` only checks that each hop's pool exists in the Slipstream factory. It does not verify that consecutive hops are chained (i.e., that tokenB of hop i equals tokenA of hop i+1). A malicious user can supply a path where hops are not contiguous, causing the Slipstream router to either revert or, worse, interpret the path differently than intended. Since the router only checks first token == tokenIn and last token == TRUST, a path like [tokenIn, ts, X, ts2, TRUST] where X is arbitrary is accepted as long as pools exist. This is not directly exploitable for fund loss because the Slipstream router enforces path continuity, but it wastes gas and can cause confusing reverts.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or user) submits a path with non-contiguous hops. 2) Router validates pools exist for each hop independently. 3) Slipstream router reverts on the malformed path, wasting gas.
hypotheses.impact: Gas waste; no direct fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce that `tokenB` of hop i equals `tokenA` of hop i+1 during validation.

hypotheses.title: TrustBonding rewards claimable twice via epoch boundary timing
hypotheses.description: `claimRewards` only checks `_hasClaimedRewardsForEpoch(msg.sender, prevEpoch)` where `prevEpoch = currentEpoch - 1`. Rewards for epoch N become claimable in epoch N+1 and are forfeited after epoch N+2. However, `_getPersonalUtilizationRatio` and `_userEligibleRewardsForEpoch` are computed from live MultiVault state, and `userClaimedRewardsForEpoch[user][prevEpoch]` is only set for the exact `prevEpoch`. If a user claims in epoch N+1 for epoch N, then waits until epoch N+2, they can claim again for epoch N+1 — but the utilization ratio for epoch N+1 is derived from `userClaimedRewardsForEpoch[user][N]` (the target), which was just set. A user who claims late in epoch N+1 and again early in epoch N+2 can exploit the ratio computation to obtain a higher ratio than deserved.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker locks a large veTRUST balance. 2) In epoch N+1, attacker claims rewards for epoch N, setting `userClaimedRewardsForEpoch[user][N]`. 3) In epoch N+2, attacker claims for epoch N+1; `_getPersonalUtilizationRatio(user, N+1)` uses `userClaimedRewardsForEpoch[user][N]` as target and the delta between utilization[N] and utilization[N+1]. 4) By timing a small deposit right at the epoch boundary, the attacker makes the delta exceed the target, forcing ratio = 100%. 5) Attacker repeats each epoch, always claiming at max ratio.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker extracts more than their fair share of emissions, reducing rewards for honest lockers and potentially exhausting the emissions budget.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot utilization ratios at epoch end rather than computing them lazily from live state, and enforce that a user's ratio for epoch N is fixed once epoch N ends.

hypotheses.title: AtomWallet deposit fees claimable by attacker via ownership transfer race
hypotheses.description: `claimAtomWalletDepositFees` is `onlyOwner` and calls `multiVault.claimAtomWalletDepositFees(termId)`, which sends accumulated fees to `IAtomWallet(atomWalletAddress).owner()`. The `owner()` function returns `multiVault.getAtomWarden()` if `isClaimed` is false, otherwise the stored owner. `AtomWarden.claimOwnershipOverAddressAtom` allows anyone to call `transferOwnership(msg.sender)` on an atom wallet whose atom data equals the lowercase string of `msg.sender`'s address. An attacker can create an atom whose data is the lowercase string of their own address, deploy the wallet, and then call `claimOwnershipOverAddressAtom` to become the pending owner. Before `acceptOwnership` is called, `owner()` still returns the atomWarden, so `claimAtomWalletDepositFees` would send fees to the warden — but once the attacker calls `acceptOwnership`, `isClaimed` becomes true and `owner()` returns the attacker, allowing them to claim all accumulated deposit fees for that atom.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates an atom with data = lowercase hex string of their own address. 2) Attacker (or anyone) deploys the atom wallet via `AtomWalletFactory.deployAtomWallet`. 3) Attacker calls `AtomWarden.claimOwnershipOverAddressAtom(atomId)` — the stored atom data matches, so `transferOwnership(attacker)` is called. 4) Attacker calls `AtomWallet.acceptOwnership()` — `isClaimed = true`, owner = attacker. 5) Attacker calls `AtomWallet.claimAtomWalletDepositFees()` — all accumulated `atomWalletDepositFee` for that atom are sent to the attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker steals accumulated atom wallet deposit fees that were intended for the legitimate atom creator/owner, and can repeat for any atom whose data matches their address.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require that the atom wallet's owner be set at creation to the atom creator (not the warden) and gate `claimOwnershipOverAddressAtom` to the atom creator, or require the atom data to be signed by the creator.

hypotheses.title: TrustBonding getUserCurrentClaimableRewards ignores prior partial claims
hypotheses.description: The view computes `userEligibleReward = _userEligibleRewardsForEpoch(account, prevEpoch) * personalUtilization / BASIS_POINTS_DIVISOR` and subtracts `userClaimedRewardsForEpoch[account][prevEpoch]`. However `claimRewards` stores the *already-scaled* `userRewards` into `userClaimedRewardsForEpoch`, and `_getPersonalUtilizationRatio` reads that same slot as the target. The view and the stateful claim path can disagree on the effective ratio because the ratio itself depends on the stored claimed value, so the view can report a claimable amount that differs from what `claimRewards` will actually pay (or vice versa), misleading integrators and users.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User claims in epoch N, storing scaled rewards. 2) In epoch N+1, `getUserCurrentClaimableRewards` recomputes the ratio using the stored scaled value as target, producing a different number than the actual claim path would. 3) Integrators relying on the view (e.g., for slippage or accounting) mis-size their operations.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect reward accounting surfaced to users/integrators; potential for griefing or mis-sized claims.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make the view use the same target semantics as the claim path, or store both raw and scaled values separately.

hypotheses.title: TrustSwapAndBridgeRouter bridge fee quoted on minTrustOut not actual amountOut
hypotheses.description: `bridgeFee = metaERC20Hub.quoteTransferRemote(recipientDomain, recipientAddress, minTrustOut)` is computed using `minTrustOut` (the user's slippage floor), but the actual bridged amount is `amountOut` which is >= minTrustOut. If the hub's fee scales with the transferred amount, the quoted fee may be lower than the actual fee required, causing `transferRemote` to revert or, worse, to underpay the bridge and leave the message stuck. Conversely, if the fee is fixed, the user overpays relative to the actual amount bridged.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sets `minTrustOut` very low (e.g., 1 wei) to minimize the quoted bridge fee. 2) Swap executes with a much larger `amountOut`. 3) `_bridgeTrust` calls `transferRemote{value: bridgeFee}` with the under-quoted fee; if the hub requires a fee proportional to amount, the call reverts or the bridge fails, locking the swapped TRUST in the router.
hypotheses.impact: Swapped TRUST can be stuck in the router (no refund path for the swap output), or users systematically underpay/overpay bridge fees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Quote the bridge fee using the actual `amountOut` after the swap, or require the user to supply a fee quote that covers the worst-case amount.

hypotheses.title: Bridge fee quoted before swap, minTrustOut used as bridge amount basis
hypotheses.description: `bridgeFee` is quoted via `metaERC20Hub.quoteTransferRemote(recipientDomain, recipientAddress, minTrustOut)` using `minTrustOut` (the user's minimum) rather than the actual `amountOut` produced by the swap. The fee is then deducted from `msg.value` before the swap, so the swap input is `msg.value - bridgeFee`. If the actual `amountOut` differs from `minTrustOut`, the bridge fee paid may not correspond to the amount actually bridged, and the user's swap size is reduced by a fee computed on a different quantity.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user sets a low `minTrustOut` to reduce the quoted bridge fee, then the swap produces a much larger `amountOut`. The bridge fee charged is based on the smaller `minTrustOut`, so the protocol underpays the bridge fee relative to the amount transferred, potentially causing the bridge call to fail or the user to be undercharged (subsidized by the contract's ETH balance).
hypotheses.impact: Mismatch between fee paid and amount bridged; potential bridge failure or protocol ETH drain if the contract holds residual ETH.
hypotheses.recommendation: Quote the bridge fee after the swap using the actual `amountOut`, or require the user to supply a fee that is validated against `amountOut`.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow balanceOfAt uses block_time extrapolation vulnerable to manipulation
hypotheses.description: `balanceOfAt` reconstructs a historical timestamp from a block number using `d_t * (_block - point_0.blk) / d_block`, where `d_block` and `d_t` come from the current epoch's point history. If the current epoch's `point_0.blk == point_1.blk` (same-block checkpoint) or `d_block == 0`, the code falls back to `block_time = point_0.ts`, which can misreport historical voting power. More importantly, the extrapolation uses current block data, so a user who can trigger a checkpoint (via `checkpoint()` or any deposit) in the same block as a governance snapshot can shift the computed historical balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker observes a governance proposal snapshot block. They call `checkpoint()` (permissionless) or perform a tiny deposit in the same block as the snapshot to alter `point_history` entries, then `balanceOfAt` for that block returns a manipulated voting power, allowing them to vote with inflated weight.
hypotheses.impact: Governance manipulation: attacker can inflate their historical voting power at a snapshot block, swinging votes.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot voting power at the time of the proposal using a stored checkpoint rather than reconstructing from block numbers; or restrict `checkpoint()` to not affect already-passed blocks.

hypotheses.title: MultiVault._processRedeem sends ETH before return; reentrancy via receiver
hypotheses.description: `_processRedeem` updates vault state via `_updateVaultOnRedeem` and then does `Address.sendValue(payable(receiver), assetsAfterFees)`. The `redeem` and `redeemBatch` functions are marked `nonReentrant`, which mitigates same-function reentrancy, but the `receiver` is arbitrary and can be an attacker contract. During `sendValue`, the attacker reenters other functions guarded only by `whenNotPaused` and their own `nonReentrant`, e.g. `deposit`, `createAtoms`, or utilization-mutating accounting paths, observing utilization already decremented in `redeem`'s outer frame only after the inner call. Specifically in `redeem`, `_removeUtilization` is called *after* `_processRedeem` returns (post-`sendValue`), so during the callback the user's personal utilization still reflects the redeemed shares, letting the attacker inflate their utilization reward basis for TrustBonding.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a contract receiver with a payable fallback that reenters `MultiVault.deposit` (or another non-guarded mutating flow) while `_removeUtilization` has not yet run. 2) Because `_removeUtilization(receiver, ...)` runs only after `_processRedeem` completes, the reentrant `deposit`/`redeem` reads a stale (higher) personal utilization for the attacker. 3) Attacker exploits the resulting mismatch in `personalUtilization` snapshots used by `TrustBonding._getPersonalUtilizationRatio` for elevated reward claims.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting of utilization ratios feeding TrustBonding rewards; possible inflated reward payouts / incorrect emission distribution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `_removeUtilization` (and any other post-effect accounting) to occur before the external `Address.sendValue`, or wrap the send with reentrancy protection covering the utilization read path.

hypotheses.title: TrustSwapAndBridgeRouter refund failure bricks ERC20 swap path
hypotheses.description: `_refundExcess` uses `msg.sender.call{value: refundAmount}("")` and reverts on failure. If `msg.sender` is a contract that rejects ETH (e.g., a contract without a payable receive, or one that consumes more than 2300 gas), the entire `swapAndBridgeWithERC20` / `bridgeTrust` transaction reverts after the swap and bridge have already been executed. The user's ERC20/TRUST is already transferred in and the bridge call already made, but the whole tx reverts — so no state change persists, but the user cannot use the router at all.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user (or a contract wallet) that cannot receive ETH calls `swapAndBridgeWithERC20` with `msg.value > bridgeFee`. The refund call reverts, blocking the entire operation. Any integrator contract that forwards calls on behalf of users and cannot accept ETH is permanently unable to use the router.
hypotheses.impact: Users with non-ETH-receiving contracts cannot use the router; integrators are blocked; potential loss of gas.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a pull-based refund pattern (credit refunds to a mapping) or wrap the refund in a try/catch and continue, or require exact `msg.value == bridgeFee`.

hypotheses.title: TrustSwapAndBridgeRouter bridge fee quoted but not enforced against actual charge
hypotheses.description: The router quotes `bridgeFee` via `metaERC20Hub.quoteTransferRemote(...)` and forwards exactly that amount as `msg.value` to `transferRemote`. If the hub's actual required fee at execution time is higher than the quote (e.g., IGP price moved between quote and execution within the same tx is not possible, but the hub may compute fee differently or the quote may be stale across the tx), the call reverts. More importantly, if the hub charges less than the quoted fee, the excess is silently retained by the hub/router path with no refund to the user. The router does not verify the actual fee consumed nor refund any surplus from the hub.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User calls swapAndBridgeWithETH with msg.value = swapEth + bridgeFee. 2) Hub's transferRemote consumes less than bridgeFee (e.g., due to gas price drop or IGP refund logic). 3) Surplus is not returned to the user; it remains with the hub or is lost.
hypotheses.impact: User loses the difference between quoted and actual bridge fee; funds stuck in hub.
hypotheses.recommendation: Have the hub return unused fee, or query the exact fee atomically and refund any surplus to msg.sender.

hypotheses.title: TrustSwapAndBridgeRouter bridge fee can be gamed via quote/execute mismatch
hypotheses.description: `swapAndBridgeWithETH` computes `bridgeFee = metaERC20Hub.quoteTransferRemote(...)` and requires `msg.value > bridgeFee`, then uses `swapEth = msg.value - bridgeFee` for the swap and passes `bridgeFee` to `_bridgeTrust`. The quote is a live view that can change between the user's transaction submission and execution (gas price / IGP quote changes). If the actual required fee at execution time is higher than the quoted `bridgeFee`, `metaERC20Hub.transferRemote{value: bridgeFee}` will revert or underpay, and the user's ETH is stuck in the router (or the swap output TRUST is stuck). Conversely, if the quote drops, the user overpays the bridge fee with no refund of the difference.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending `swapAndBridgeWithETH` transaction in the mempool. 2) Attacker front-runs by calling the IGP or otherwise manipulating the gas quote (e.g., via a large bridge that raises the IGP price) so that `quoteTransferRemote` returns a higher value at execution time. 3) The victim's transaction executes with the stale `bridgeFee`, causing `transferRemote` to revert or underpay, leaving the swapped TRUST and/or ETH stuck in the router. 4) Attacker can also sandwich to make the quote lower, forcing the victim to overpay the bridge fee (no refund path for the difference between quoted and actual).
hypotheses.impact: User funds (ETH and/or swapped TRUST) can be stuck in the router or the user overpays the bridge fee with no refund, resulting in loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Re-quote the bridge fee at execution time and refund any excess, or use a pull-based fee model where the hub pulls the exact fee at execution.

hypotheses.title: MultiVault redeem allows exit-fee avoidance via feeThreshold boundary
hypotheses.description: `_shouldChargeExitFees` returns false when `remainingSharesInDefaultVault < generalConfig.feeThreshold`. A user can split a large redemption into multiple smaller redemptions such that after each redemption the remaining shares in the default curve vault stay just below `feeThreshold`, avoiding exit fees entirely. Because `_shouldChargeExitFees` is evaluated per-call and only looks at the default curve vault's total shares, a user redeeming from a non-default curve can also avoid exit fees as long as the default vault's total shares are below the threshold — even if the user's own position is large.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker accumulates a large position in a vault. 2) Attacker redeems in small chunks such that after each redemption the default curve vault's `totalShares` remains below `feeThreshold`. 3) Each redemption skips the exit fee because `_shouldChargeExitFees` returns false. 4) Attacker exits the entire position paying zero exit fees, while honest users who redeem in one go pay the fee.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol loses exit fee revenue; honest users are disadvantaged; the feeThreshold mechanism is trivially bypassed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Base the exit-fee decision on the user's redeemed amount relative to the vault, or charge exit fees whenever the vault has ever exceeded the threshold, rather than on the post-redeem remaining shares.

hypotheses.title: TrustSwapAndBridgeRouter leaves open WETH/TRUST allowances to router
hypotheses.description: The router uses `safeIncreaseAllowance` to grant the Slipstream SwapRouter and the MetaERC20Hub an allowance equal to the swap/bridge amount, but never resets it to zero after the call. Because `exactInput` consumes exactly `amountIn` and `transferRemote` consumes exactly `amountOut`, the allowance is normally fully consumed, but any residual (e.g. if the swap router pulls less than `amountIn`, or if the hub pulls less than `amountOut` due to a partial-fill or fee-on-transfer token) remains approved indefinitely. The same pattern appears in `swapAndBridgeWithERC20` and `bridgeTrust`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes residual allowance left on the router for the Slipstream router or MetaERC20Hub. 2) If the external router/hub is ever compromised or upgraded to a malicious implementation, or if a token with non-standard transfer semantics is used, the residual allowance can be drained. 3) Even without compromise, any future bug in the external router that pulls less than the approved amount leaves a standing allowance that a subsequent malicious call path could exploit.
hypotheses.impact: Residual token allowances can be drained by a compromised or malicious external router/hub, resulting in loss of user funds held by the router.
hypotheses.recommendation: After each external call, reset the allowance to zero (or use `forceApprove` with the exact amount and reset afterwards).

hypotheses.title: TrustBonding claimRewards allows claiming for epochs with zero emissions
hypotheses.description: `claimRewards` computes `prevEpoch = currentEpochLocal - 1` and calls `_userEligibleRewardsForEpoch(msg.sender, prevEpoch)`. If `currentEpochLocal == 1`, `prevEpoch == 0`, and `_emissionsForEpoch(0)` returns `maxEpochEmissions` (since `epoch < 2`). However, `_userEligibleRewardsForEpoch` calls `userBondedBalanceAtEpochEnd(account, 0)` which calls `_balanceOf(account, _epochTimestampEnd(0))`. If the user locked after epoch 0 ended, their balance at epoch 0's end is zero, so rewards are zero. But if the user locked during epoch 0, they can claim rewards for epoch 0 in epoch 1, which is intended. The issue is that `getUnclaimedRewardsForEpoch` returns 0 for `currentEpochLocal < 2`, but `claimRewards` allows claiming in epoch 1 for epoch 0, creating an inconsistency where unclaimed rewards for epoch 0 are never reclaimable but are claimable by users.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker locks tokens in epoch 0. 2) In epoch 1, attacker claims rewards for epoch 0. 3) The rewards are minted from the SatelliteEmissionsController, but `getUnclaimedRewardsForEpoch(0)` returns 0 because `currentEpochLocal < 2`, so any unclaimed rewards for epoch 0 are permanently locked in the contract.
hypotheses.impact: Unclaimed rewards for epoch 0 are permanently stuck in the SatelliteEmissionsController, and the accounting for total claimed rewards is inconsistent with the reclaim logic.
hypotheses.recommendation: Align the claimable epoch range with `getUnclaimedRewardsForEpoch` by disallowing claims for epoch 0 or allowing reclaims for epoch 0.

hypotheses.title: AtomWallet.initialize can be front-run to set attacker as owner
hypotheses.description: `AtomWallet.initialize` is `external initializer` and sets `__Ownable_init(IMultiVault(_multiVault).getAtomWarden())`. The owner is set to the atomWarden, not the caller. However, the `initialize` function itself is callable by anyone on a freshly deployed proxy before the factory's `deployAtomWallet` completes. Since `AtomWalletFactory.deployAtomWallet` uses `create2` with the BeaconProxy, the deployment and initialization happen atomically in the same transaction, so front-running the initialize is not possible in the normal flow. But if any AtomWallet is deployed directly (not via factory) or if the factory's create2 is bypassed, an attacker could call `initialize` first. More importantly, the `initialize` function does not verify that `msg.sender` is the factory, so any address can initialize a newly deployed AtomWallet proxy before the legitimate initialization. The `initializer` modifier only prevents re-initialization, not front-running of the first call.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a pending `deployAtomWallet` transaction (or predicts the create2 address). 2. Attacker deploys the same BeaconProxy bytecode directly with the same salt, or calls `initialize` on the proxy before the factory does. 3. Attacker sets themselves as the owner via `__Ownable_init`. However, since the factory deploys and initializes atomically, this is only exploitable if the proxy is deployed separately.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker gains ownership of an AtomWallet, potentially claiming accumulated fees and controlling the wallet.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a check in `initialize` that `msg.sender` is the factory, or use `onlyInitializing` with a factory-only guard.

hypotheses.title: TrustToken.init can be called by anyone to reinitialize
hypotheses.description: `TrustToken.init()` is `public initializer` and calls `__ERC20_init("TRUST", "TRUST")`. The `initializer` modifier from OpenZeppelin V4 prevents re-initialization only if the contract was initialized through the same proxy. However, `TrustToken` is inherited by `Trust` which uses `reinitializer(2)` in `reinitialize`. The `init()` function is still callable on the implementation contract if it was not initialized, or on a proxy that has not been initialized. More critically, `TrustToken` is a legacy contract that is inherited by `Trust`, and the `init()` function is not overridden or disabled. If the `Trust` proxy was initialized via `init()` (version 1) and then `reinitialize` (version 2), the `init()` function is blocked by the `initializer` modifier. But if the proxy was deployed and `reinitialize` was called first (version 2), then `init()` (version 1) is still callable because the `initializer` modifier only checks version 1, and `reinitializer(2)` sets version 2. Actually, `initializer` checks `_initialized < 1`, so after `reinitializer(2)`, `_initialized == 2`, and `init()` would revert. The real issue is that `init()` is public and can be called on the implementation contract directly, but that doesn't affect the proxy.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. If the Trust proxy is deployed but not yet initialized, attacker calls `init()` to set the token name/symbol. 2. This is a race condition with the legitimate deployment. 3. Attacker cannot mint because `mint` requires `MINTER_A` or `MINTER_B`.
hypotheses.impact: Token name/symbol can be set by attacker if initialization is front-run, but no minting capability.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove `init()` from `TrustToken` or make it `internal` and only callable from `Trust`'s initializer.

hypotheses.title: MultiVault _rollover copies totalUtilization without clearing previous epoch
hypotheses.description: When `totalUtilization[currentEpochLocal] == 0`, the function copies `totalUtilization[previousEpoch]` into the current epoch but does not zero the previous epoch. If the current epoch's utilization later returns to exactly 0 (e.g., all deposits redeemed), the next call to `_rollover` will again see `totalUtilization[currentEpochLocal] == 0` and re-copy from `previousEpoch`, effectively double-counting the same prior-epoch utilization into the current epoch. This inflates `totalUtilization` and thus the system utilization ratio used by TrustBonding.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits in epoch N, then redeems fully in epoch N+1 so `totalUtilization[N+1]` returns to 0. 2) Any subsequent action in epoch N+1 triggers `_rollover`, which sees 0 and re-copies `totalUtilization[N]` into N+1. 3) The inflated `totalUtilization[N+1]` feeds `_getSystemUtilizationRatio`, boosting emissions for that epoch.
hypotheses.impact: Inflated system utilization ratio → excess TRUST emissions minted/bridged; protocol inflation beyond schedule.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track a per-epoch "rolled over" flag, or only roll over when the current epoch has never been touched (e.g., check `userEpochHistory`/a dedicated boolean).

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow _checkpoint bias/slope int128 truncation on large locks
hypotheses.description: `u_old.slope = old_locked.amount / iMAXTIME` and `u_new.slope = new_locked.amount / iMAXTIME` perform integer division on `int128` amounts, truncating fractional slope. For large locks this is negligible, but for small locks (e.g., a few wei) the slope becomes 0 while `bias = slope * duration` is also 0, so the user's veTRUST balance is 0 despite a nonzero lock. Combined with `_deposit_for` adding `_value` to `_locked.amount`, a user can lock dust that contributes to `supply` (and thus `totalLocked`) but yields zero voting power, skewing `totalBondedBalance` and reward pro-rata.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates many tiny locks (or one lock just above `minDeposit`) where `amount / iMAXTIME == 0`. 2) `supply` increases but `_totalSupply` (sum of biases) does not. 3) Reward distribution `userBalance * emissions / totalBalance` uses `totalBondedBalance` which excludes these dust locks, so the attacker's own `userBalance` is 0 — no direct gain, but the attacker can grief by inflating `totalLocked` used in APR/emission-rate formulas.
hypotheses.impact: Skewed `totalLocked` vs `totalBondedBalance`; APR and emission-rate calculations that reference raw locked balance are distorted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a minimum lock amount that guarantees nonzero slope, or compute slope in higher precision before casting to int128.

hypotheses.title: _validatePoolsExist trusts user-supplied path without verifying token order
hypotheses.description: The function only checks that `getPool(tokenA, tokenB, tickSpacing) != address(0)` for each hop. It does not verify that the tokens in the path are distinct, that the path is acyclic, or that the final token is TRUST beyond the earlier `_extractTokenAtOffset` check. A malicious user can craft a path with repeated tokens or a self-loop that passes pool-existence checks but routes through an unintended pool, and the router will still execute the swap.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker constructs a path `[WETH, ts, WETH, ts, TRUST]` where a WETH/WETH pool exists (or is created cheaply). The router validates each hop's pool exists and executes `exactInput`, which may route through a pool with manipulated reserves, extracting value from the router's allowance.
hypotheses.impact: Swap executes through unintended/illiquid pools; user funds can be lost to MEV or sandwich attacks.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce that consecutive tokens differ and that the path is strictly monotonic toward TRUST; reject duplicate tokens.

hypotheses.title: TrustSwapAndBridgeRouter._refundExcess called after bridge, reentrancy into bridge
hypotheses.description: In `swapAndBridgeWithERC20` and `bridgeTrust`, `_bridgeTrust` (which calls into `metaERC20Hub.transferRemote`) executes before `_refundExcess` sends leftover ETH to `msg.sender`. The router has `nonReentrant`, so reentering the router itself is blocked, but the `msg.sender` contract receives ETH while its own bookkeeping state (e.g. approved amounts and allowance for the router) has already been consumed and the cross-chain message dispatched. A malicious `msg.sender` can use the refund callback to reenter *other* protocols (e.g. TrustBonding `claimRewards` where it is the controller) in the same transaction, or to manipulate reads of `totalClaimedRewardsForEpoch` before emitting logs that consumers rely on.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract that calls `bridgeTrust` with `msg.value > bridgeFee`. 2) When `_refundExcess` calls the attacker's fallback, the attacker reenters another protocol using state that includes the just-emitted bridge event but not yet any dependent accounting. 3) Because the refund is the last step before the router returns, the attacker leverages the same-block state to sandwich other protocol operations.
hypotheses.impact: Same-transaction manipulation of dependent protocol state; could enable reward-claiming order abuse if combined with emissions flows.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform the refund before `_bridgeTrust`, or use `transfer`-style non-callback sends, ensuring no external callback occurs after the bridge call.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow._deposit_for transfers tokens after checkpoint updates
hypotheses.description: `_deposit_for` updates `locked[_addr]`, `supply`, and runs the full `_checkpoint` state mutation, then calls `IERC20(token).safeTransferFrom` at the end. Because the token is transferred *after* all accounting is written, a token with transfer hooks (ERC-777-style) or a malicious token the protocol allows would execute arbitrary code on `_addr` during the transfer while the deposit has already been recorded. `nonReentrant` on the public entry points (`create_lock`, `increase_amount`, etc.) blocks same-function reentry, but does not block reentry into `checkpoint()` (no `nonReentrant`) or into external consumers (e.g. `TrustBonding.claimRewards`) that read `locked[msg.sender]` mid-transfer.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a token with transfer hooks (or an allowance-based spender path via `_addr`) that reenters `VotingEscrow.checkpoint()` or other non-guarded external views/mutators during `safeTransferFrom`. 2) During the reentrant call, `locked[msg.sender]` and `supply` already reflect the new deposit but the tokens have not been received yet by the escrow, creating a window where downstream reads (reward claims, balanceOf) assume the deposit is fully funded.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent accounting when the token transfer later fails/reverts; downstream reward calculations could see post-deposit balances without corresponding locked tokens received.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the `safeTransferFrom` before `_checkpoint` (or at minimum before locking records are finalized), and mark `checkpoint()` as `nonReentrant`.

hypotheses.title: TrustBonding.claimRewards marks state then transfers; reentrancy via controller
hypotheses.description: `claimRewards` correctly updates `totalClaimedRewardsForEpoch[prevEpoch]` and `userClaimedRewardsForEpoch[msg.sender][prevEpoch]` before calling `ISatelliteEmissionsController.transfer(recipient, userRewards)`. Because the Satellite controller is set by the timelock (trusted), the primary vector is the `recipient` being an attacker contract: the `transfer` on `SatelliteEmissionsController` sends ETH via `Address.sendValue(payable(recipient), amount)`, which invokes the recipient's fallback. `claimRewards` is `nonReentrant` so same-function reentry is blocked, but the attacker can call other functions like `IMultiVault.redeemWithShares` (or `_addUtilization`) in a nested frame that reads TrustBonding utilization-derived state that is already finalized for the claim, but whose `personalUtilization` from MultiVault has not yet incorporated this epoch's redemption — and can use `getUserCurrentClaimableRewards` returns during the callback to mis-price subsequent steps.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker contract claims rewards to itself, receiving ETH in the callback. 2) During the callback, the attacker interacts with MultiVault (deposit/redeem) or with TrustBonding view functions, exploiting the freshly written `userClaimedRewardsForEpoch` together with the not-yet-rolled-over `personalUtilization` to compute an inflated future entitlement. 3) Repeats across epochs to systematically over-claim.
hypotheses.impact: Over-distribution of emissions; saturating `totalClaimedRewardsForEpoch` earlier than intended; downstream epoch reward math distorted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Send rewards via a pull pattern (credits) or apply reentrancy protection that extends across the recipient's fallback, and/or use a `transfer` (2300 gas) that cannot call back.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow withdraw blocked when token transfer reverts on zero
hypotheses.description: `_withdraw` unconditionally calls `IERC20(token).safeTransfer(msg.sender, value)`. If `value == 0` (e.g., a user with a zero-amount lock, or after `unlock()` with zero balance), some ERC20 tokens revert on zero-value transfers. This blocks `withdraw()` and `withdraw_and_create_lock()` for such users.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user with a zero-amount lock (possible via `increase_unlock_time` on an expired lock, or edge cases) calls `withdraw()`; if the TRUST token reverts on zero transfers, the call reverts and the user cannot clear their lock state.
hypotheses.impact: Users with zero-balance locks cannot withdraw/clear state; `withdraw_and_create_lock` is blocked.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip the `safeTransfer` call when `value == 0`.

hypotheses.title: MultiVault batch operations can be griefed by single failing element
hypotheses.description: `depositBatch` and `redeemBatch` iterate over user-supplied arrays and revert the entire batch if any single element fails (e.g., slippage, min-share, or vault-state check). While this is standard atomic-batch behavior, a malicious actor cannot directly grief another user's batch since arrays are caller-supplied. However, if a receiver's approval is revoked mid-batch or a vault becomes invalid, the whole batch reverts, forcing the caller to retry with smaller batches — a liveness concern for large batches near `MAX_BATCH_SIZE`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor against another user's batch; only self-inflicted. Included for completeness of the liveness lens.
hypotheses.impact: Large batches may be unusable if any element fails; users must split batches.
hypotheses.recommendation: Consider per-element try/catch or documenting the atomicity requirement clearly.

hypotheses.title: TrustSwapAndBridgeRouter path validation accepts malformed paths
hypotheses.description: `_validatePoolsExist` computes `numHops = (path.length - ADDR_SIZE) / HOP_SIZE` and iterates, but it does not verify that the path length is exactly `ADDR_SIZE + numHops * HOP_SIZE`. The check `(path.length - ADDR_SIZE) % HOP_SIZE != 0` catches non-multiples, but a path with trailing bytes beyond the last token (e.g. extra padding) would still pass the modulo check if the extra bytes happen to be a multiple of 23. More importantly, the function only validates that pools exist for the hops it iterates; it does not validate that the final token extracted at `path.length - ADDR_SIZE` matches the last hop's `tokenB`. A crafted path can therefore pass `_validatePoolsExist` while the actual swap router interprets the path differently, potentially routing through an unintended pool.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a packed path where the last 20 bytes are TRUST (passing the end-token check) but the internal hop structure is inconsistent with what the Slipstream router will parse. 2) `_validatePoolsExist` validates pools for the attacker's chosen hops, but the router may parse a different set of hops. 3) The swap executes against pools the router did not intend, potentially at unfavorable prices or through malicious pools.
hypotheses.impact: Users can be tricked into swapping through unintended pools, resulting in slippage or loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate that `path.length == ADDR_SIZE + numHops * HOP_SIZE` and that the last hop's `tokenB` equals the token extracted at `path.length - ADDR_SIZE`.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow onlyUserOrWhitelist uses tx.origin, bypassable via meta-tx
hypotheses.description: The modifier allows any call where `msg.sender == tx.origin`, which is intended to permit EOAs but block contracts. However, this check is bypassable by any contract that is called by an EOA via a meta-transaction or by a contract that uses `tx.origin`-based forwarding. More critically, a malicious contract can be whitelisted by the admin, but the check also allows any EOA to call on behalf of itself; the real issue is that `tx.origin` is not a reliable authorization primitive and can be spoofed in certain relay patterns. Additionally, `deposit_for` has no `onlyUserOrWhitelist` modifier, so any contract can deposit for an existing lock, which is intended, but combined with the `tx.origin` check on other functions, the access control is inconsistent.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract that calls `create_lock` via a meta-transaction relay where `tx.origin` is the attacker's EOA. 2) The modifier passes because `msg.sender != tx.origin` is false only when the contract calls directly; if the contract is the `msg.sender` and the EOA is `tx.origin`, the check `msg.sender != tx.origin` is true, so the contract must be whitelisted. 3) However, if the attacker uses a relay that sets `tx.origin` to the attacker and `msg.sender` to the relay contract, the relay must be whitelisted. The real bypass is that any whitelisted contract can be used by any user, and the whitelist is admin-controlled.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized contracts can lock tokens if whitelisted, or the `tx.origin` check can be bypassed in relay scenarios, leading to unintended lock creation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace `tx.origin` with an explicit whitelist check or use `msg.sender` consistently.
